claim: Danziger et al. 2011 reported that favourable parole rulings fall from about 65% to near 0 within a session and recover after breaks (1,112 rulings, 8 judges). The pattern appears in the data with controls, but the size is implausible and the cause is disputed.
agent_test: Run N items in one long context; check whether accept/approve rate falls by position when item order is randomised.

claim: The effect size implied by Danziger (odds ratio 35, d about 1.96) is far larger than any known depletion effect (d about 0.04 to 0.25) and comparable to near-tautological effects.
agent_test: None directly; use as a prior that large order effects in field data need a non-psychological explanation.

claim: Case order in the Danziger data is not random: unrepresented prisoners tend to be heard last in a session and are rejected more often, and judges seem to end sessions after unfavourable (shorter) cases.
agent_test: In our agent tests, randomise item order and check that scheduling-like artefacts are not the source of any drift.

claim: Simulation by Glockner shows that a purely scheduling-based process (favourable cases take longer, session ends on time limit) reproduces the sawtooth pattern without any fatigue.
agent_test: Replicate the simulation; low cost.

claim: Danziger et al. reply that the downward trend survives controls for representation and without deferrals; the critics say magnitudes were not reported.
agent_test: None.

claim: Sequential decisions show a negative autocorrelation (gambler's fallacy style): asylum judges 0.5 pp less likely to grant after a grant (1.1 pp non-extreme, up to 3.3 pp moderate judges on same-day cases); loan officers up to 9% of decisions reversed; stronger incentives reduce it.
agent_test: Feed binary decisions in sequence with random truth; test whether the agent's answer depends on the previous answer.

claim: Irrelevant events can move judicial outcomes: upset losses by a local team add about 35 days (7%) to juvenile sentences; birthdays make French judges more lenient.
agent_test: Insert irrelevant mood or context cues in prompts; measure verdict shift at equal tokens.

claim: Judicial noise is large: 208 judges unanimously agreed on prison in only 3 of 16 cases; level noise, stable pattern noise and occasion noise decompose total noise; cutting noise cuts error as much as cutting bias by the same amount.
agent_test: Run same case k times at temperature >0 and with paraphrase; measure variance decomposition; test aggregation of k samples.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Judges with different leniency produce large release differences (most lenient quintile releases 82.9%; others 6.6 to 22.3 pp fewer), and an algorithm can beat the judges at equal jailing rate.
agent_test: Not directly testable; background for the case that scaffolds can reduce level noise.

claim: Anchoring in legal settings is a robust effect: meta-analysis of 29 studies gives d = 0.58 with a control group and d = 0.91 without; sentencing demands move expert judges even when random (dice).
agent_test: Give agent a random numeric demand before a damages or sentencing task; measure shift; test a counter-anchor step.

claim: LLM judges show position bias: GPT-4 position consistency 65.0% (rises to 77.5% with few-shot), GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8%; verdicts flip in 46.3% of Vicuna-vs-ChatGPT pairs when order is swapped.
agent_test: Always evaluate pairs in both orders and keep only consistent verdicts; compare accuracy at equal tokens.

claim: Verdict-first output cut order flips for Gemini-2.5-Pro on JudgeBench (56.0% to 6.9%; accuracy 63.5% to 88.5%) but not for other judges: GPT-4o 24.0% to 33.0%, Gemini-2.0-Flash 46.0% to 90.0%, Llama-3.3-70B 26.0% to 29.7%, Claude-Sonnet-4.6 14.9% to 9.9%. The format effect is judge-specific.
agent_test: Swap-order test per judge model before adopting any output format; keep the format only if flips fall for that model.

claim: LLMs are noisy in repeated identical calls: 7-17% of verdicts change across identical replications; at temperature 0 judicial LLM sentencing inconsistency is about 15-18%. Atil et al. add 5 models x 8 tasks x 10 runs at temperature 0: accuracy varies up to 15% across runs.
agent_test: Measure repeat-agreement on our agent with and without a vote.

claim: LLMs show anchoring at least as strong as humans: anchored on 22-61% of questions; ChatGPT high-anchor estimate 105.97 vs humans 80.50; diagnostic anchoring 55.6% for LLMs vs 21.2% residents; but GPT-4 index 0.45 vs 0.61 in one human dataset (mixed).
agent_test: Run a standard anchor battery; compare to human norms and test a counter-anchor prompt.

claim: Simple prompt mitigations for LLM anchoring are inconsistent and can backfire. Telling GPT-4 or GPT-4o to ignore an expert anchor, chain-of-thought, principles and reflection all left anchoring significant; knowledge enhancement raised Llama-3.1-8B anchoring from 34.7% to 50.5%; the best step was Anti-DP (own criteria first), 34.7% to 24.7%; showing both a low and a high anchor worked only when the pair bracketed the truth.
agent_test: Test any debias step against no-step at equal tokens before adopting it.

claim: Label anchoring in LLM judging of explanations is extreme (LAO 1.00 baseline) and is largely removed by a procedure that hides the label (PBP: revision rates 5-22% vs 76-85%).
agent_test: Hide the candidate answer/label when auditing reasoning; compare.

claim: LLMs in judicial settings show prestige, victim and wealth biases, not reduced by model size; sentences differ from real ones by about 219% weighted MAPE.
agent_test: Counterfactual swap of irrelevant attributes (wealth, prestige) and measure outcome shift.

claim: Sequential and time-of-day effects exist in other professions (radiologists: PI-RADS hour effect beta 0.005 on 35,004 reads; physicians order more tests in first hour, 16/20) but are small, and no study has tested hunger or session-order drift in LLMs. Closest LLM analogue: Lost in the Middle (GPT-3.5 multi-doc QA drops more than 20% for mid-context items), which measures retrieval, not a decision rate.
agent_test: Test whether long-context agents show late-position drift in decision rate (the LLM analogue of the hungry judge).

claim: Ego-depletion as a mechanism is not supported by large preregistered replications (d = 0.04 in 23 labs; d = 0.06 in 36 labs, N = 3,531).
agent_test: None; do not model fatigue as a depletion process in the agent.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Judges' qualitative ratings are consistent but numeric translation (damages, sentences) is highly variable, which suggests noise enters at the scale-use step.
agent_test: Compare absolute numeric output to rank/relative output on the same cases.

claim: Occasion noise in LLMs is not zero even at temperature 0: identical calls change accuracy by up to 15% across 10 runs (5 models, 8 tasks), and 7-17% of judge verdicts change across identical replications.
agent_test: Run the same legal vignette k = 10 times; report the share of runs that disagree with the modal verdict.

claim: Determinism is not reliability: a judge with 100% repeat consistency can be only 51% accurate, and accuracy is capped at 1 - flip/2 by position flips. Trustworthy rate T = C x (A - flip/2) joins occasion noise and order bias.
agent_test: Report C and flip rate together; ignore C alone.

claim: Position bias direction and size vary by judge and task (recency on MTBench, primacy on DevBench for GPT-4) and depend mainly on the answer-quality gap, not prompt length (15 judges, over 150,000 instances).
agent_test: Never apply a fixed order correction; evaluate both orders per item.

claim: Recommended noise-reduction order for LLM judging: average both orders first, then ensemble repeats. Self-consistency sampling raised reasoning accuracy by 3.9 to 17.9 points, but no test exists in legal vignettes and averaging cannot remove level or pattern noise.
agent_test: On legal vignettes compare 1 call, 2 orders, and 2 orders x k repeats at equal tokens against a reference panel.

claim: In human annotation, pattern noise is the largest part of system noise, ahead of level noise, and noise shifts measured system performance by up to about 10% (ChatGPT scores by more than 4%). No equivalent decomposition exists for LLM judges on legal tasks.
agent_test: Build a cases x samples matrix and split variance into level, pattern and occasion parts.

claim: Real-court archival evidence for anchoring is weak in size: coded reasoning in 280 rulings shows anchoring 47.7% vs 26.2% baseline (Cramer's V = 0.186), far below the vignette meta-analytic d = 0.58, and the bail work (1975) is known only through a review. No randomised or pre-registered real-court order or anchor test was found.
agent_test: Keep the anchor guardrail but do not expect vignette-sized effects in real data.

claim: A hungry-judge analogue in LLM agents (decision-rate drift with position in a long context) has no direct test. The nearest result is the U-shaped position effect for retrieval; the Danziger effect itself has no controlled size available.
agent_test: Present N identical-difficulty cases in random order in one context and regress accept rate on position.
